The morning sky suggested the day was going to be bright and cloudless. Instead the fields, as far as the eye could see, were shrouded by a shifting mass 
of dark clouds high above. Curious, the Traveler sits on a stone outcropping and begins to sketch the rhythmic forms the cloud took. From so far away it 
looked like it was moving slowly, undulating and twisting upon itself...perhaps it was moving too fast for a cloud.
 
A small trilling chirp catches the Travelers attention and, on the rock next to them, a green feathered bird with a long, trailing, pink tail hops closer. 
Putting down their pencil they watch the tiny bird hop closer and closer before it opens its oddly jagged beak and takes a bite at their pants.
  
Yelping in surprise the Traveler swats at the bird, it flutters away with a high pitched trill. Feeling apologetic for the violent outburst, the Traveler returns 
to their book for only a moment before hearing an echoing trill from up above, and then another, and another, within mere moments the air began to 
vibrate with a deafening screech of trilling hundreds. Quickly looking to the dark sky, the Traveler sees the unnatural cloud spin and twist into a vortex, 
and as it descends closer to them, thousands upon thousands of birds begin to materialize from the cloud of darkness.
Ordinarily found near the prairies that skirt the edges of the Wealdwoods, the diminutive hummingbird flutters about from flower 
to flower, its green shimmering feathers as welcome as a calm and peaceful summer day. That all changes quickly when spring warms 
the grasses and a keening death knell is heard screeching across the open skies of the Farplains. Before long, thousands of them gather 
into a great murmur, darkening the sky above the flat lands, becoming a natural calamity and blocking out the sun. A single maedrynn 
hummingbird may be of little threat, but during the ferocious but fortunately short mating season, they become an absolute apex 
predator together. Countless birds descending like a tornado of serrated beaks onto any creature that is foolish enough to be out in 
the open daylight, ripping and flensing flesh from bone in a frantic need to fuel their rapid and voracious metabolism. Unlike most 
hummingbirds, the maedrynn can lay several eggs at once. With the mother unable to fly back and forth to feed so many hatchlings, 
they line their nests with layers of meat so that the hungry young can feast immediately. Once the fledglings have tested their wings 
and fluttered away from the nest, the hummingbirds return to a diet of sugary flower nectar and the multitude of insects and arachnids 
that the teeming Farplains can easily provide.
Many lands suffer annual storms, seasonal floods and reoccurring natural calamities. Nature adapts to the rhythm and uses these 
waves of destruction as a means of cleansing. The Farplains have done much the same with the maedrynn murmurs and their seasonal 
voracious storm of death.
 
While most of the Farplains' ecosystem would consider the tyrandroth as its apex predator, and for many seasons of the year it is, from 
the wide arid plains of the Grayfynn to the rich fields of Valedayn, the maedrynn reigns supreme as an absolute force of nature, if only 
for a destructive sliver of time. When the chill of winter abates and the flowers bloom in spring's heat, the maedrynn flock en mass 
from the outer edges of the fields and prairies, their trilling birdsong changing for something more aggressive, more screeching as they 
rapidly build in size and temperament. For the creatures that migrate across the plains, this begins as a pestering annoyance as solitary 
birds take nipping bites. But as the days of amassing hummingbirds continue, they begin to build up into great flocks, descending on 
the creatures in a ripping frenzy.
 
Triggering migrations and mobilizing the young and healthy away from the swarming carnivores, the maedrynn inadvertently clear 
out the weak and provoke many creatures to move to greener pastures. While this leads to the long term benefit of both the species 
and the land, it is hard to feel that when the swarm of birds rip through the creatures savagely. Thousands upon thousands glittering, 
green feathered bodies flock to the sky, their murmurs beautiful to behold in the great shifting mass, like a single body it flows across 
the sky like liquid, the males and females of their kind dancing and frolicking together in mesmerizing aerial dances, until they spot 
movement. The dark cloud above condenses into a twisting tornado, descending on the rushing prey in a storm of feathers and beaks. 
Akin to aerial piranha, the hummingbirds tear into the flesh of the terrestrial beasts, their serrated beaks flensing fur and hide with 
ease, a shrilling cacophony of chirps only matched by the screams of pain by the beast within their feathered vortex. Sated and flying 
off to lay their nest with strips of meat, the bones of the remains settle into the soil, left to fertilize the fields with its rich phosphorous 
and calcium. Once the eggs are lain and the nest properly prepared with meat, the bird can be quite friendly and curious, chirping 
delightfully as it flutters from flower to flower, completely dissimilar to the ravenous maelstrom it once was.
The maedrynn murmurs are truly a sight to behold, beautiful in their ferocity but, like a storm, it is best seen from afar. Travelers 
stepping on to the Farplains often must contend with ferocious lizards, gigantic insects and more. Choosing to journey during the brief 
reign of the maedrynn is a recipe for annihilation, leaving little but bones for the grass.
